description.p: Splitlane is a native terminal workspace for running coding agents in parallel. Launch Claude Code, Codex, opencode, Pi, or any CLI agent in real panes, keep each session visible, and react when one needs input.
Features:

ul.li: One-click coding-agent launchers with per-session status tracking
Horizontal and vertical split panes with drag-to-resize, up to 32 panes
Branch-aware workspaces with rename, quick-switch, and session restore
In-app Git diff viewer and branch review prompts for agents
MCP bridge so capable agents can read other panes without copy/paste
JSON-RPC 2.0 IPC for local automation and integrations
Native Rust/GPUI rendering with Wayland and X11 support on Linux

description.p: Each agent session started in a git repository gets its own branch and worktree, so two sessions never edit the same checkout. Closing a session with work in its branch asks whether to keep it, and saves a snapshot before deleting it. Hovering a session's row lists what you wrote in it, and the History tab searches everything you wrote in old sessions, including those that ran in a worktree. Codex and other sessions opened from history resume instead of starting empty, and the theme follows the OS appearance until you choose one.

A phone follows the agent sessions on the computer and answers them, from a page at splitlane.dev/app added to its home screen. Pair it in Settings, Phone, by scanning a code and typing the six digits the phone shows. Everything between the phone and the computer is encrypted end to end through a relay that forwards it unread, and it works while the window is closed. A session that takes up its next turn by itself now tells the session that opened it about each end.

With the window closed, the command-line tool still answers for the agent sessions the session host keeps: it lists them with what the window last saw, reads their output, returns an agent's last answer, sends text when writing was allowed at launch, and waits for a turn to end from the agent's own reports. A session kept with no pane opens in a pane of its own project when no pane is open.

A Running sheet lists every agent session and every command running in a shell, with a way to go to each or stop it. Quitting counts commands running in shells as work, names them, and offers to review them first; sessions kept running are mentioned on the next launch. Active only keeps a shell while a command runs in it.

The Activity chip shows how many agent sessions are failed, waiting and running, and its list now includes the running ones, with a way to jump to each. An Active only filter hides the sessions nothing is happening in. The TLS library used for updates is updated for four security advisories.

On macOS and Linux, agent sessions outlive the window: they run in a process of their own, so quitting with the sessions kept, an update and a crash of the window leave them working, and the next start shows each in its pane again. On Linux, keeping the sessions is now the default when quitting. A lead agent is told when a session it opened finishes even if that took only seconds, and the context meter no longer takes an idle compaction for the size of the context window.

Quitting no longer has to stop your agents: with agent sessions open the window is put away and they keep working. Starting Splitlane while it is running brings its window forward. On macOS, commands whose answer is longer than 8 KiB no longer fail. A lead agent whose own waiting went wrong is still told that a session it opened has finished.

Codex sessions report their state again, and a Codex session can open sessions and work through them. A script or a scheduled job can start an agent on a task with nothing set up first, from a directory of an open project. A finished run is no longer reported as longer than it took.

A working agent is now green and an agent waiting for you is amber, and focus is shown without colour. A session is told when a session it opened ends its turn. Notifications about a waiting agent or a broken session play the system sound. On macOS a Codex session can open and read other sessions once you allow it in Settings.
A terminal left one column wide inside a full-width pane is now put back to its size within a few seconds on macOS, and every size sent to a terminal is recorded for diagnosis.

A Claude Code session opened by another session no longer declines its task as pasted text, a question an agent asks before its first prompt shows as waiting, "splitlane add" reports what became of the prompt, and updates can be checked for on request.

A lead agent now hears when a session it opened has finished, "splitlane ps" and "status" report agent sessions, "splitlane read" returns the screen as well as the history, and panes keep their script names across a restart.
On macOS the app can update itself again: earlier versions refused every release and have to be replaced by hand once.

An agent in a pane can open agent sessions of its own and work through them: each is a row in the rail under the one that opened it, and a session that is waiting for you says so in a notification whichever way Splitlane learned of it. The skill that teaches Claude Code and Codex the commands is installed at every start.

Updates are checked for while the app stays open, a worktree is removed when its project closes if nothing in it would be lost, and background git no longer runs programs named by a repository's own configuration.
Codex and Claude Code no longer show as running before their first message, and every package ships the licenses of its dependencies.
Free access for agents can now be turned on only from Settings, not by editing the config file.
A freshly started agent without hooks no longer shows as running until its first message, and the window has a title on Linux.
First Splitlane release.
